title: Jack and the Beanstalk

evidence.note: Wikipedia's article says: 'RKO attempted to renew the film's copyright in 1980, but as Jack and the Beanstalk was first copyrighted in 1951, the renewal should have occurred in 1979, 28 years after the original copyright. As a result, the film entered the public domain.' This is an unverified Wikipedia claim. I have not checked the 1951 copyright date, so I do not say that any renewal was late. If the original registration was in 1952, a 1980 renewal would be on time. The same article names Exclusive Productions as the production company and Warner Bros. as distributor, not RKO. I did not check the registration year, the claimant or any renewal against a Catalog of Copyright Entries volume or the Copyright Office record. The print status is undetermined, and nothing here shows the film is in the public domain.

evidence.note: The Internet Archive item description says Jack is babysitting Donald, a child prodigy. Jack's attempt to lull the boy to sleep by reading the fairy tale 'Jack and the Beanstalk' aloud fails. Donald reads the story instead, Jack falls asleep, and he dreams that he is the young Jack of the fairy tale. The item credits the screenplay to Nat Curtis and Pat Costello. I have not cited a source for the age or copyright term of the fairy tale, so this layer is not marked verified. The screenplay is part of the print layer.

Wikipedia cites a ClassicFlix product page for this. I could not load ClassicFlix or Kickstarter to confirm the dates or what the release adds. Any added material, such as new titles, commentary or extras, may be protected, but I did not verify what the release contains.

editorial:
Jack and the Beanstalk (1952) is an Abbott and Costello comedy. Exclusive Productions made it and Warner Bros. distributed it. It premiered in New York on April 7, 1952, with Heinz Roemheld credited for the music. Nat Curtis and Pat Costello wrote it. In a babysitting framing story, Jack falls asleep while a child reads the fairy tale aloud, and he dreams that he is the young Jack of the tale. Wikipedia says the opening and closing segments are in sepia and the main part was filmed in Eastmancolor and shown in the SuperCinecolor process.

The print status is undetermined. Wikipedia says the film was first copyrighted in 1951 and that RKO attempted a renewal in 1980. It says the renewal should have come in 1979 and that the film entered the public domain as a result. That is an unverified Wikipedia claim. I have not checked the copyright year. If the film was first registered in 1952, a 1980 renewal would be on time, so I do not call any renewal late. The same article names Exclusive Productions and Warner Bros., not RKO. I could not confirm any of it from the Catalog of Copyright Entries or the Copyright Office. Do not treat the film as public domain until you have checked the records yourself. A renewal search covering 1978 to 1981 has not yet been done.

The score status is undetermined. Per Wikipedia, unverified, a 2020 Kickstarter campaign funded a Blu-ray restoration, and ClassicFlix released it on July 26, 2022. I could not confirm this from ClassicFlix or Kickstarter. The release may add protectable material.
faq: Is Jack and the Beanstalk (1952) free to use?

Unknown. The print status is undetermined. Wikipedia claims an RKO renewal was attempted in 1980 and that the film entered the public domain. I could not verify that, the 1951 copyright date or the claimant in any primary record. If the copyright date was 1952, a 1980 renewal would be on time. Check the original registration and renewals for 1978 to 1981 in the Copyright Office records and the Catalog of Copyright Entries. I have not established the copyright term of the fairy tale itself.
Can I use the ClassicFlix restoration or the Internet Archive copy?

I did not check the rights status of either copy. Per Wikipedia, unverified, ClassicFlix released a restoration in 2022. If it did, it may include protectable additions such as new titles or bonus material. If you want to avoid that material, use a copy without those additions. The Internet Archive item page makes no copyright statement.
